tEn: David Silver & Lasse Espeholt on Building a Superlearner for the Age of Experience
tZh: David Silver 与 Lasse Espeholt：为经验时代打造超级学习者
sEn: David Silver and Lasse Espeholt of Ineffable Intelligence discuss why learning from experience, not LLMs, is the path to superintelligence.
sZh: Ineffable Intelligence 的 David Silver 与 Lasse Espeholt 探讨为何从经验中学习、而非大语言模型，才是通往超级智能的道路。

consensus.en: Superintelligence will emerge from systems that learn and discover knowledge autonomously from experience.
consensus.zh: 超级智能将源于能够从经验中自主学习和发现知识的系统。

consensus.en: Current LLM paradigm relies on human data and human-in-the-loop, limiting true autonomous discovery.
consensus.zh: 当前的大语言模型范式依赖人类数据和人类在环，限制了真正的自主发现。

consensus.en: Simulation is the safest and fastest place to build and understand superintelligence.
consensus.zh: 模拟是构建和理解超级智能最安全、最快速的地方。

consensus.en: Alignment approaches based on human language and data are reaching their limits.
consensus.zh: 基于人类语言和数据的对齐方法正在达到其极限。

consensus.en: Compute is a major driver, and scaling laws apply to reinforcement learning with adjustments.
consensus.zh: 算力是主要驱动力，缩放定律适用于强化学习但需调整。

consensus.en: Pacing frontier AI in the real world while accelerating research in simulation is prudent.
consensus.zh: 在现实世界中放缓前沿AI，同时在模拟中加速研究是审慎的。

contrarian.en: Human language is not the optimal medium for reasoning; more expressive neural approaches exist.
contrarian.zh: 人类语言不是推理的最佳媒介；存在更具表现力的神经方法。

contrarian.en: Giving up human data and priors leads to faster and greater discovery, as shown by AlphaZero.
contrarian.zh: 放弃人类数据和先验会带来更快、更伟大的发现，如AlphaZero所示。

contrarian.en: Simple reward functions in complex environments can yield emergent complexity, not handcrafted rewards.
contrarian.zh: 在复杂环境中，简单的奖励函数可以产生涌现复杂性，而非手工设计的奖励。

contrarian.en: Superintelligence can be built entirely in simulation, enabling faster and safer development.
contrarian.zh: 超级智能可以完全在模拟中构建，从而实现更快、更安全的开发。

contrarian.en: Monitoring chain of thought in English will become insufficient as agents grow more powerful.
contrarian.zh: 随着智能体变得更强大，用英语监控思维链将变得不足。

contrarian.en: A small team with high compute per person can outperform larger organizations in breakthrough research.
contrarian.zh: 人均算力高的小团队在突破性研究中可以胜过更大的组织。

turns.en: Collectively, we started with this kind of gray mush in our head. We somehow started out knowing nothing at all and somehow discovered everything that humans know today. It was this process of collective discovery—of languages, technology, science, mathematics, and all the rest of it. Everything we learned, we discovered for ourselves. That's an incredible thing that no one has cracked yet in AI. To me, that is the essence of what it will take to get to superintelligence: a system that can just keep learning and discovering knowledge forever.
turns.zh: 我们集体从头脑中这团灰色的糊状物开始。我们不知怎么地一开始一无所知，却不知怎么地发现了今天人类所知的一切。这是集体发现的过程——语言、技术、科学、数学等等。我们学到的一切，都是我们自己发现的。这是 AI 至今尚未破解的不可思议之事。对我来说，这就是实现超级智能的本质：一个能够永远不断学习和发现知识的系统。

turns.en: I'm thrilled to have Dave Silver and Le Espol with us, two of the co-founders of Ineffable Intelligence. Great name, by the way. Fun fact, Dave, you were the first person I cold emailed to come on Training Data when we started the show a hundredish episodes ago, and it feels like a full circle moment to finally have you on the show. So thank you for joining us.
turns.zh: 我非常高兴邀请到 Dave Silver 和 Le Espol，Ineffable Intelligence 的两位联合创始人。顺便说一句，名字很棒。有趣的是，Dave，大约一百集前我们刚开始做节目时，你是我第一个冷邮件邀请来上 Training Data 的人，现在终于请到你，感觉像是一个圆满的轮回。所以感谢你的加入。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.en: Dave, let's start with you. Your 2009 PhD was on reinforcement learning applied to the devilishly difficult game of Go. You demonstrated for the world for the first time that superhuman in one domain machine intelligence was possible, and I think you were really the figure that inspired the entire current generation of reinforcement learning and deep learning researchers. So thank you for your contributions to where the field is. I'm curious, thinking back to that point in time, what did you learn? What did you have conviction on, and what has remained the same and what has changed as AI has changed over the last 5 years or so?
turns.zh: Dave，我们从你开始。你 2009 年的博士论文是关于将强化学习应用于极其困难的围棋游戏。你首次向世界证明，在某一领域实现超越人类的机器智能是可能的，我认为你正是激励了当前整整一代强化学习和深度学习研究者的那个人。所以感谢你对这个领域发展的贡献。我很好奇，回想那个时候，你学到了什么？你当时坚信什么？在过去 5 年左右 AI 的变化中，什么保持不变，什么改变了？

turns.en: Yeah, thank you and pleasure to be here and I'm glad I finally made it after these hundred episodes. It's a pleasure to be here. So I suppose I always had this conviction starting my PhD and going into the game of Go that the right approach to solve AI was through learning from experience, through systems that discovered things for themselves, that were learning through reinforcement learning to get better and better and better, and that would be the thing which would lead to the emergence of intelligence and ultimately superintelligence. So I suppose we were able to show that in the game of Go, but it's a conviction that has held true throughout my career. And here we are now applying that conviction at Ineffable, trying to show that indeed superintelligence can emerge all the way through systems that learn from experience. And in terms of things which are different, although we are not pursuing the human data path that the LLM world has pursued, I do think there's lots of interesting lessons to learn from that. In particular, it was definitely a surprise to me how a system that was trained on a massive amount of data could then be very quickly fine-tuned on a very small amount of data to kind of completely change its behavior. That was something which I think changed my mindset in terms of just suggesting that if you get things at the right scale, a lot of things which seem like incredibly hard or like they might be very slow—once you've experienced enough data, after that the things that were slow can become very fast. I think that's a lesson that wasn't obvious to me in advance until it happened.
turns.zh: 是的，谢谢，很高兴来到这里，我很高兴在一百集之后终于来了。很高兴来到这里。我想我从读博开始进入围棋领域时就一直坚信，解决 AI 的正确方法是通过从经验中学习，通过那些自己发现事物的系统，通过强化学习不断变得更好，而这将导致智能乃至超级智能的出现。我想我们在围棋中证明了这一点，但这个信念贯穿了我的整个职业生涯。现在我们正在 Ineffable 应用这个信念，试图证明超级智能确实可以通过从经验中学习的系统涌现出来。至于不同之处，虽然我们没有走 LLM 世界所走的人类数据路径，但我确实认为从中可以学到很多有趣的教训。特别是，一个在大量数据上训练的系统竟然可以很快地在很少的数据上微调，从而完全改变其行为，这对我来说绝对是个惊喜。我认为这改变了我的思维方式，它表明如果你把事情做到正确的规模，很多看起来极其困难或可能非常缓慢的事情——一旦你经历了足够的数据，之后那些缓慢的事情就可以变得非常快。我认为这是一个我事先并不明显的教训，直到它发生了。

transcript.sec: Decision to Start a New Lab

turns.en: Okay, we're going to come back to that later. You could have run this program inside DeepMind, where you could have probably had more access to compute than just about anybody. You decided the right thing to do was to start a new lab. Why'd you do that?
turns.zh: 好的，我们稍后会回到这一点。你本可以在 DeepMind 内部运行这个项目，在那里你可能比几乎任何人都能获得更多的算力。你决定正确的做法是成立一个新实验室。你为什么这么做？

turns.en: Yeah. So look, first of all, I had a fantastic time at DeepMind. I loved my years there and I have a huge amount of respect for the people there and still got on with them very well. But at the end of the day, I have a really strong belief about how we can go beyond where we are today with AI and all the way to superintelligence, and the path that I believe in doesn't actually go through LLM-based products as an intermediate point. And when I really thought about that, I thought about it really hard. I realized that I felt that so passionately that this deserved to be more than just the corner of an organization that's focused on LLM-based products and deserved to be represented by an elite AI lab that really just gives this approach its all and represents it 100%. And once I realized that, it felt very natural to create this company. I suppose another way to look at it is that the world already has tens of thousands if not hundreds of thousands of really talented researchers all pursuing exactly the same approach, really just doubling down on LLMs with pre-training, post-training, coding, and that kind of LLM path. Am I going to be the one person that's pursuing that approach? Is that the most effective use of my time and my energy? In the end, I realized that there's this other lamppost that right now no one is looking under, and where if I actually put my effort there, has a much higher chance of really having a massive impact on the field, because if this works, it's going to change the whole of AI. So I think that realization also meant that this was something which just means that it's the best way to have impact upon the field through this approach.
turns.zh: 是的。首先，我在 DeepMind 度过了非常美好的时光。我喜欢在那里的岁月，我对那里的人怀有极大的敬意，并且仍然与他们相处得很好。但归根结底，我坚信我们如何能够超越当今 AI 的水平，一路走向超级智能，而我所相信的路径实际上并不经过基于 LLM 的产品作为中间点。当我真正思考这一点时，我思考得非常认真。我意识到我对此感受如此强烈，以至于这值得不仅仅是一个专注于基于 LLM 产品的组织的一角，而值得由一个精英 AI 实验室来代表，真正全力以赴地投入这种方法，100% 地代表它。一旦我意识到这一点，创建这家公司就变得非常自然。另一种看待方式是，世界上已经有成千上万甚至数十万真正有才华的研究人员都在追求完全相同的方法，真的只是在 LLM 上加倍投入，包括预训练、后训练、编码以及那种 LLM 路径。我会成为那个追求这种方法的人吗？那是我的时间和精力的最有效利用吗？最终，我意识到还有另一盏路灯，目前没有人在下面寻找，而如果我真的把努力放在那里，就更有可能对该领域产生巨大影响，因为如果这成功了，它将改变整个 AI。所以我认为这种认识也意味着，这是通过这种方法对该领域产生影响的最佳方式。

turns.en: Plus, you had a company name that couldn't go to waste.
turns.zh: 另外，你有一个不能浪费的公司名字。

turns.en: That's right. Yeah.
turns.zh: 没错。是的。

turns.en: You want to say where the name Ineffable came from?
turns.zh: 你想说说 Ineffable 这个名字的由来吗？

turns.en: Yeah. So, I suppose the name Ineffable came from this idea that knowledge could be so incredible—like the things which superintelligence will one day discover, this knowledge, it's going to be so unbelievable, incredible, and it's going to be something which is profoundly amazing and perhaps so profound that we can't even express it in human language. And so really, it's like, you know, in line with this other path that doesn't go through human language-based approaches, but instead builds systems that discover things for themselves and has the possibility to discover knowledge that's unbelievably profound and ultimately ineffable.
turns.zh: 是的。所以，我想 Ineffable 这个名字来自这样一个想法：知识可以如此不可思议——就像超级智能有一天会发现的东西，这种知识将如此令人难以置信、不可思议，它将是某种深刻惊人的东西，也许如此深刻，以至于我们甚至无法用人类语言来表达。所以真的，就像，你知道，这与另一条路径一致，那条路径不经过基于人类语言的方法，而是构建自己发现事物的系统，并有可能发现令人难以置信地深刻、最终不可言说的知识。

turns.en: I should say there was also a secret second reason that we used, which was this idea that it really has to work. If you really just double down on learning from experience, it's an approach that just has to work. So you could say that it can't possibly fail. So it's ineffable. So there you go, there's the secret reason as well.
turns.zh: 我还应该提一下，我们当时还有一个秘密的第二个理由，就是这个想法：它真的必须能行得通。如果你真的只是加倍押注于从经验中学习，这是一种必须能行得通的方法。所以你可以说它不可能失败。所以它就是不可言喻的（ineffable）。所以就是这样，这就是那个秘密理由。

turns.en: Amazing, best lab name. Um, Lei, what about you? You were at Google, you were in a different group than Dave, in the deep learning group at DeepMind, and you spent years scaling up reinforcement learning on GPUs. What made you decide to leave DeepMind and what drew you to co-found Ineffable?
turns.zh: 太棒了，最好的实验室名字。嗯，Lei，你呢？你之前在 Google，你和 Dave 在不同的组，在 DeepMind 的深度学习组，你花了多年时间在 GPU 上扩展强化学习。是什么让你决定离开 DeepMind，又是什么吸引你来共同创办 Ineffable？

turns.en: Right. Yeah, so I joined DeepMind in January 2015, and actually I started working a bit with Dave around 2016, where I was doing this work on scaling up reinforcement learning. So as you said, I was part of the deep learning team and he was leading a reinforcement learning team, but we were working on an internal project together. I actually left DeepMind twice. So I left DeepMind in summer 2018 and went to Google Brain. Then eventually Google Brain and DeepMind merged and then I was back again. But then I left DeepMind again like a year before Dave left. And the first time I heard about Ineffable was actually through one of our eventual investors reaching out to me asking what I thought about Dave. Well, my first reaction was, damn, I missed out on an opportunity. I should have reached out to him. But I recall Dave as more often than not being one of the smartest people in the room. And shortly after that sync with that investor, they actually reached out to me. So it was great. Yeah, so I really love to work with Dave. I knew Wojtek and Chris from back in the day and I thought the team was great and I also thought it's amazing to have an opportunity like this in Europe. It should be said as well that we worked together on some of the early approaches to combining reinforcement learning with deep learning and trying to scale things up. And it should be said that Lassa, who by the way is very modest, but he actually worked on some of the original approaches that were the first attempts to actually scale up reinforcement learning and show that it could be done at large scale, and ways to parallelize reinforcement learning and ways to build out architectures that were scalable. And if you look today at the way the field's gone, actually all of the ideas that people use today kind of hail back to those original work that Lassa did back in the day. That's where all the roots come from of scaled up RL. So he was the first to figure it out.
turns.zh: 对。嗯，我 2015 年 1 月加入 DeepMind，实际上我大概在 2016 年开始和 Dave 一起工作，当时我在做扩展强化学习的工作。所以就像你说的，我当时在深度学习团队，他领导强化学习团队，但我们一起做一个内部项目。我实际上离开过 DeepMind 两次。我在 2018 年夏天离开 DeepMind 去了 Google Brain。后来 Google Brain 和 DeepMind 合并了，我又回来了。但后来我在 Dave 离开前一年又离开了 DeepMind。我第一次听说 Ineffable 其实是通过我们后来的一位投资人联系我，问我怎么看 Dave。嗯，我的第一反应是，该死，我错过了一个机会。我应该主动联系他的。但我记得 Dave 往往是房间里最聪明的人之一。和那位投资人同步后不久，他们实际上联系了我。所以很棒。是的，我真的很喜欢和 Dave 一起工作。我早就认识 Wojtek 和 Chris，我觉得这个团队很棒，我也觉得在欧洲有这样的机会太棒了。还应该说的是，我们一起研究过一些早期将强化学习和深度学习结合的方法，并试图扩大规模。还应该说的是，Lassa，顺便说一句他非常谦虚，但他实际上研究了一些最初的方法，这些是最早尝试真正扩大强化学习规模并证明可以在大规模上做到的方法，以及并行化强化学习的方法和构建可扩展架构的方法。如果你看看今天这个领域的发展，实际上人们今天使用的所有想法都可以追溯到 Lassa 当年做的那些原创工作。这就是扩展 RL 的所有根源。所以他是第一个搞明白的人。

turns.en: Wonderful. We should have you guys introduce each other instead of you're both too humble to brag about yourselves. Okay, let's talk about Ineffable and what you're building. You have a beautiful mission statement as a company. You want to build a superlearner and make first contact with superintelligence. Can you define both of those things for us? What is a superlearner and what does making first contact look like?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们应该让你们互相介绍，而不是你们都太谦虚不好意思自夸。好，我们来谈谈 Ineffable 和你们在构建的东西。你们公司有一个很美的使命宣言。你们想构建一个超级学习器（superlearner），并与超级智能进行第一次接触。你能为我们定义这两件事吗？什么是超级学习器，第一次接触又是什么样的？

turns.en: Yeah. So to me a superlearner is something which has incredible capacity both in its depth of what it can learn and in its breadth. So in the depth dimension, it should be something that can start from not knowing anything at all and can go all the way through to discovering things that go way beyond what humans know. So an analogy to this would be the way that humans collectively, we started with this kind of gray mush in our head. We somehow started out knowing nothing at all and somehow discovered everything that humans know today was this process of collective discovery of languages and technology and science and mathematics and all the rest of it. Everything we learned, we discovered it for ourselves. It wasn't that someone came down and gave us a blueprint of how this should work and it wasn't that someone came down and gave like a trillion element data set of, oh, this is what these things should look like. We actually figured it out for ourselves and that's an incredible thing that no one has cracked yet in AI. And so to me that is the essence of what it will take to get to superintelligence, like a system that can just keep learning and discovering knowledge forever. So the second element is breadth, that we want something which can do this incredible discovery all the way to incredible things and it should be possible to drop it into any stream of experience. So whether it's a simulated world or a digital world or a physical world, whatever it's dropped into, it should be something that can just learn and learn and learn. So that's the dream. I think if we crack this, then to me it gives rise to a superintelligence that will be like encountering magic. It will be something which is so profoundly amazing that it will be able to do wonderful things.
turns.zh: 是的。所以对我来说，超级学习器是一种在它能学到的深度和广度上都具有惊人能力的东西。所以在深度维度上，它应该能够从一无所知开始，一路发现远超人类所知的东西。一个类比是人类集体，我们从脑子里这种灰色的糊状物开始。我们不知怎么地从一无所知开始，不知怎么地发现了今天人类所知的一切，这是一个集体发现的过程，包括语言、技术、科学、数学等等。我们学到的一切，都是我们自己发现的。并不是有人下来给了我们一张蓝图，告诉我们这应该怎么运作，也不是有人下来给了我们一个万亿元素的数据集，说这就是这些东西应该是什么样子。我们实际上是自己搞明白的，这是 AI 中还没有人破解的不可思议的事情。所以对我来说，这就是达到超级智能的本质，一个可以永远学习和发现知识的系统。第二个要素是广度，我们希望它能进行这种不可思议的发现，一直到不可思议的事情，并且应该能够把它投入到任何经验流中。所以无论是模拟世界、数字世界还是物理世界，无论它被投入到什么中，它都应该能够不断地学习、学习、再学习。所以这就是梦想。我认为如果我们破解了这一点，那么对我来说，它会产生一种超级智能，就像遇到魔法一样。它将是如此深刻惊人，能够做出美妙的事情。

turns.en: What will it feel like when we first encounter it? Or is it one of these things where you can't predict ahead of time?
turns.zh: 当我们第一次遇到它时，会是什么感觉？还是说这是那种你无法提前预测的事情？

turns.en: I think it will be amazing. I think we will have an experience of wonderment. And the only thing I can say from my own experience is what happened when we got to this point in admittedly much narrower fields. But when we got there in board games, when we got to the point of superhuman play in the game of Go, it brought wonderment to the field. The Go players who saw AlphaGo playing, they were amazed and it was a joyful experience for them to witness this kind of Go playing. Same happened when we got to superhuman play in chess and the chess players, they were so excited. And just imagine going far beyond that but in things which are discovering incredible things, new fields of science, new types of technology that we've never even dreamed of. I mean it will be incredible.
turns.zh: 我认为会非常惊人。我认为我们会体验到惊奇。从我自己经验中唯一能说的是，当我们在公认狭窄得多的领域达到这一点时发生了什么。但当我们在棋盘游戏中达到这一点时，当我们在围棋中达到超人水平时，它给这个领域带来了惊奇。看到 AlphaGo 下棋的围棋棋手们，他们惊叹不已，见证这种围棋下法对他们来说是一种快乐的体验。当我们在国际象棋中达到超人水平时也是一样，棋手们非常兴奋。想象一下远远超越这一点，但在发现不可思议的事情、新的科学领域、我们从未梦想过的新型技术方面。我的意思是，那将是不可思议的。

turns.en: So the current paradigm, these large language models with reinforcement learning seem to be at least knocking out millennium problems and making some sorts of scientific discoveries. Does that count as a superlearner or what's the difference between something that can make novel scientific discoveries versus a superlearner in your sense of the term?
turns.zh: 那么当前的范式，这些带有强化学习的大型语言模型似乎至少能解决千禧年问题并做出某种科学发现。这算超级学习器吗？还是说能做出新颖科学发现的东西和你所说的超级学习器有什么区别？

turns.en: Yeah, so look, I think LLMs are doing a lot of great things and I have a lot of respect for what's being achieved.
turns.zh: 是的，你看，我认为 LLM 正在做很多伟大的事情，我对所取得的成就非常尊重。

turns.en: What I mean by a super learner is something which first of all discovers completely autonomously. And I think what we've seen so far, at least with these kind of approaches that have been taken, is there's a lot of human-in-the-loop effort that's required to make these breakthroughs. It's not fully autonomous yet. And it's also something which should be applicable to real-world embodied domains where the agent can learn from its physical experience. And we're a long, long, long way off that, and it's not at all clear that LLMs and language-based approaches are even the right vehicle to achieve that kind of knowledge. Thinking about these things in terms of language might not even be the right paradigm, and it might just be that all of this human data that's being used in LLMs is kind of weighing things down. So a lot of respect for some of the progress that's made, but I don't think we're anywhere close to this true super learner of something which can autonomously just discover everything for itself.
turns.zh: 我所说的超级学习者，首先是指能够完全自主发现新知识的东西。就目前采取的那些方法来看，我们看到的仍然需要大量人类在环的努力才能取得突破，还没有完全自主。而且它应该适用于真实世界的具身领域，让智能体能够从物理经验中学习。我们距离那一步还非常非常遥远，而且完全不清楚 LLM 和基于语言的方法是否真的是实现那种知识的正确载体。用语言来思考这些事情可能根本不是正确的范式，也许 LLM 中使用的所有这些人类数据反而在拖后腿。所以我对已经取得的进展非常尊重，但我认为我们离真正的超级学习者——那种能自主发现一切的东西——还差得很远。

transcript.sec: Building the Super Learner in Practice

turns.en: What does building this look like in practice for you? And you know, we backed Giannis who was on your original AlphaGo team and he told us that, you know, one of the things that's distinct about you is you can have these incredibly ambitious visions, but you also ground the team in very practical research milestones. And I'd love to understand big big big vision. What does this look like in the day-to-day and what are you implementing? How do you spend your days right now?
turns.zh: 对你来说，实际构建这个东西是什么样的？我们投资了 Giannis，他原来在你的 AlphaGo 团队，他告诉我们，你的一个独特之处在于，你既能拥有极其宏大的愿景，又能让团队扎根于非常实际的研究里程碑。我很想了解，宏大的愿景，在日常中是什么样子，你在实现什么？你现在每天是怎么度过的？

turns.en: Yeah, great question. So day-to-day, I suppose there's a lot of hard technical work with people like Lassa to build the whole stack that means we've got a state-of-the-art reinforcement learning stack that allows us to run things at massive scale, inhale data in the optimal way, be able to learn and have systems that keep learning and learning and learning. And then on top of that, so we've spoken about the super learner, the other aspect which we're building is we're building out environments which are capable of super learners like discovering everything, like simulated environments in which a super learner can discover everything that we mean by intelligence. We call those crucibles. So they're environments in which it's possible for agents to make incredible discoveries, in which it's possible to express and learn everything that we think of as intelligence. And so we have been putting a certain amount of effort into creating these environments. And so it's a combination of building out the super learner, doing the research to make super learners incredible and beat the state-of-the-art of what's possible with reinforcement learning, both in terms of the engineering and the research that happens, and creating and placing the super learners into these crucibles to see the emergence of incredible behaviors. And in terms of the grounding, you asked about how to ground this in the day-to-day. So we ground it in milestones, and the milestones are analogous to what happens with the human journey, where we discovered incredible things, and so those become natural milestones for our agents to rediscover the great moments that humans went through in our discovery of knowledge.
turns.zh: 是的，好问题。日常来说，我想有很多艰难的技术工作，像 Lassa 这样的人在构建整个技术栈，这意味着我们有一个最先进的强化学习栈，能让我们大规模运行、以最优方式吸收数据、能够学习，并拥有不断学习的系统。然后在此基础上，我们谈到了超级学习者，我们正在构建的另一个方面是环境，能够进行超级学习者式的发现一切，比如模拟环境，在其中超级学习者可以发现我们所说的智能的一切。我们称这些为“熔炉”。所以这些环境让智能体有可能做出不可思议的发现，有可能表达和学习我们认为是智能的一切。我们一直在投入一定的精力来创建这些环境。所以这是构建超级学习者、进行研究使超级学习者变得不可思议并超越强化学习现有水平的结合，既包括工程也包括研究，以及创建并将超级学习者放入这些熔炉中，看到不可思议行为的涌现。至于扎根，你问如何在日常中扎根。我们将其扎根于里程碑，这些里程碑类似于人类历程中发生的事情，我们发现了不可思议的事物，所以这些成为我们的智能体重新发现人类在知识发现过程中经历的重要时刻的自然里程碑。

transcript.secZh: 在实践中构建超级学习者

turns.en: What do you think the agents will rediscover first when that's going to be your first moment of oh this is working?
turns.zh: 你认为智能体首先会重新发现什么？那将是你的第一个“哦，这起作用了”的时刻？

turns.en: I imagine we're going to be surprised. I think one thing which is different about the way we take to doing reinforcement learning to a lot of the rest of the field is that we're not breadcrumb trailing the particular objective to be learned about. A lot of the way people do RL with LLMs at the moment is to say oh you know the agent should be learning about this problem and then this problem and this problem and after following that trail we're kind of pulling the agent by its nose towards a particular desired outcome. We're not taking that approach. We're giving the agent some simple objectives and asking it to discover things that will surprise us and amaze us. So, you know, the agent is in principle capable of discovering all kinds of things and we don't necessarily know in advance what those discoveries will be and it's kind of just going to be exciting to witness that journey. So I hope to be surprised I think is the answer to your question.
turns.zh: 我想我们会感到惊讶。我认为我们在强化学习方法上与许多其他领域的不同之处在于，我们不会用面包屑引导特定的学习目标。目前很多人用 LLM 做强化学习的方式是，哦，智能体应该学习这个问题，然后这个问题，再这个问题，沿着那条路径，我们牵着智能体的鼻子走向特定的期望结果。我们不采取这种方法。我们给智能体一些简单的目标，要求它发现会让我们惊讶和惊叹的东西。所以，原则上智能体能够发现各种事物，我们不一定事先知道那些发现会是什么，见证这段旅程将会非常令人兴奋。所以，我希望感到惊讶，我想这就是你问题的答案。

turns.en: Interesting. So what you're saying is instead of explicitly giving the agent the goal to go rediscover language or build a calculator or build a computer, you're going to give it other more open-ended goals and the agent may discover that the most efficient way to actually or the best way to actually accomplish that goal may be to build some of these tools that we as humans have already built. Is that one way of putting it?
turns.zh: 有趣。所以你的意思是，不是明确给智能体一个目标去重新发现语言或建造计算器或建造计算机，而是给它其他更开放的目标，智能体可能会发现，实际上最有效或最好的方式来完成那个目标，可能是建造一些我们人类已经建造的工具。这是一种说法吗？

turns.en: That's one way of putting it. I think another way to say it is people often think in RL, oh my god, how do I come up with a reward function that perfectly specifies this really complicated thing that I want to discover, like how can I specify exactly what I mean by science or how can I specify exactly what I mean by interesting maths. But there's an alternative, and the alternative is to give the agent something really straightforward to optimize, but in a really complex environment where there's a lot to learn about. And so it turns out that if you look at the way the world has worked in nature, the pursuit and optimization of a very simple, easy-to-describe quantity can often give rise to incredibly hard-to-describe complexity and emergence. So examples of that would be evolution, which just optimizes survival of the fittest or some kind of fitness signal, and the pursuit of fitness gave rise to all of the complexity that we see in life. In the human journey, the pursuit of relatively simple goals that we as humans have gave rise to all of the complex behaviors that humans ultimately acquired and all of the knowledge that we eventually ended up with. So the emergent complexity is much greater than the starting point that it was given. So it wasn't like evolution said, look, hey humans, here's this idea of science and you need to get to the most complex science that's out there. It was really something much simpler.
turns.zh: 这是一种说法。我认为另一种说法是，人们在强化学习中经常想，天哪，我如何想出一个奖励函数，完美地指定我想发现的这个非常复杂的东西，比如我如何精确指定我所说的科学，或者如何精确指定我所说的有趣的数学。但有一种替代方案，就是给智能体一些非常直接可优化的东西，但在一个非常复杂、有很多东西要学的环境中。事实证明，如果你看看自然界中世界运作的方式，对非常简单、易于描述的量的追求和优化，往往会产生极其难以描述的复杂性和涌现。例子就是进化，它只是优化适者生存或某种适应度信号，而对适应度的追求产生了我们在生命中所看到的所有复杂性。在人类历程中，对人类相对简单目标的追求，产生了人类最终获得的所有复杂行为以及我们最终拥有的所有知识。所以涌现的复杂性远大于起始点。并不是进化说，嘿人类，这是科学的概念，你需要达到最复杂的科学。它其实要简单得多。

transcript.secZh: 开放式目标与涌现复杂性

turns.en: A way to describe this might be that humans, in pursuit of our goals, started coordinating a bit more. In the process of coordinating, we discovered that it was helpful to start communicating. In the process of communicating, we started trading. In the process of trading, we discovered that basic arithmetic was useful. Then we discovered that tools were useful. Then we discovered that some basic science was required to understand how the tools would work, which gave rise to more complex technology. Understanding the technology required more complex maths, and so forth. So all in the pursuit of relatively simple goals, this incredible complexity emerged. If we can get that process right, things are going to take off and lead to unbelievable things.
turns.zh: 描述这个过程的一种方式是：人类在追求目标的过程中，开始更多地协调。在协调的过程中，我们发现沟通很有帮助。在沟通的过程中，我们开始交易。在交易的过程中，我们发现基础算术很有用。然后我们发现工具有用。接着我们发现需要一些基础科学来理解工具如何运作，这催生了更复杂的技术。理解技术又需要更复杂的数学，如此循环。所以，在追求相对简单的目标时，这种不可思议的复杂性涌现了出来。如果我们能把这个过程做对，事情就会起飞，带来难以置信的成果。

turns.en: It's fascinating. Are the rewards for your agents similar to human biology and evolution, like trying to make it to the next generation? What does a reward function look like for you all?
turns.zh: 这很迷人。你们智能体的奖励机制是否类似于人类生物学和进化，比如努力延续到下一代？你们的奖励函数是什么样的？

turns.en: Yeah, we've been experimenting with quite a number of different rewards. So it's not like we have one answer to that question. But I think one thing we're not doing is crafting a reward that exactly describes what we mean by science, or exactly what we mean by technology, or exactly what we mean by language. We expect our agents to discover things. And if we can't crack that, if we can't crack this problem as AI scientists, we're never going to have agents that discover whole new fields of knowledge that we don't even know about. There are vast fields that will exist that we don't even know have the potential to exist at this point in time. Imagine you were back in the days of Newtonian physics and no one even knew that quantum physics was a thing, or that relativity was a thing. We should be in that process of open-minded discovery where our agents are free to figure things out for themselves. And I think that's going to lead to much more exciting outcomes.
turns.zh: 是的，我们一直在尝试多种不同的奖励。所以并不是说我们对这个问题只有一个答案。但我认为我们没做的一件事是：精心设计一个能精确描述我们所说的科学、技术或语言的奖励。我们期望智能体自己去发现事物。如果我们无法解决这个问题，作为 AI 科学家，我们就永远无法拥有能发现全新知识领域的智能体，那些我们甚至不知道存在的领域。在当下，有些广阔的领域将会存在，但我们甚至不知道它们有存在的潜力。想象一下回到牛顿物理学的时代，没人知道量子物理或相对论的存在。我们应该处于那种开放心态的发现过程中，让智能体自由地自己弄清楚事情。我认为这会带来更令人兴奋的成果。

turns.en: What do these crucibles look like in practice? You're contrasting it to today when people say environments—often it's a set of tasks and what the agent should have done on the task. It sounds like your environments, your crucibles, are very different. What do they look like in practice?
turns.zh: 这些“熔炉”在实践中是什么样的？你把它和今天人们所说的环境做了对比——通常是一组任务以及智能体在任务中应该做什么。听起来你们的环境、你们的熔炉非常不同。它们在实践中是什么样的？

turns.en: So we are building crucibles which, without giving too many details away, have the capacity for a lot of emergent complexity. The key thing about them is that it's not like we've handcrafted a whole load of puzzles for the agents to work with. There's just a huge amount of emergent complexity there. Some of that emergent complexity can come from different places. It can come from physics engines that give rise to complexity as you've got millions of interacting objects with a complex physics engine. You can have millions of interacting agents, and the world becomes much more complex because it suddenly now includes the complexity of all those other agents within the world that the agents are building. So there are ways to build worlds that are vastly more complex than the standard simulators like Atari 57 or whatever people have been working with in the past, and which are certainly more complex than the standard benchmark tasks that people are using. And if you get that right, you have a world in which there's the possibility for discovery by the agent. There's the possibility for the agents to discover everything from technology to science to mathematics to languages to everything else. Just the same way humans, all the way through from more basic things like motor control or coordination—the whole spectrum is possible.
turns.zh: 我们正在构建的熔炉，在不透露太多细节的情况下，具有大量涌现复杂性的能力。关键之处在于，我们并没有手工制作一大堆谜题让智能体去解决。那里有大量的涌现复杂性。其中一些涌现复杂性可以来自不同地方。它可以来自物理引擎，当你拥有数百万个相互作用的物体和复杂的物理引擎时，就会产生复杂性。你可以有数百万个相互作用的智能体，世界会变得更加复杂，因为它突然包含了智能体所构建的世界中所有其他智能体的复杂性。所以，有办法构建比标准模拟器（比如 Atari 57 之类的）复杂得多的世界，这些世界肯定比人们使用的标准基准任务更复杂。如果你做对了，你就拥有了一个智能体有可能发现事物的世界。智能体有可能发现从技术到科学、数学、语言等一切事物。就像人类一样，从更基础的运动控制或协调，整个谱系都是可能的。

turns.en: Like if you look at a game like Go, which is very simple to represent—it's just a bit map. The simulation is extremely simple. But you still see this emerging behavior of something complex. It's super interesting to us. So of course Go is way simpler than what we can imagine doing. But at the same time, going all the way to 100% realistic physics would be very computationally expensive. So we want to create this range of crucibles where we have simple ones that can execute quickly and we can iterate on, but where we can still see very complex behavior.
turns.zh: 就像看围棋这样的游戏，它非常容易表示——只是一张位图。模拟极其简单。但你仍然看到复杂行为的涌现。这对我们来说超级有趣。所以当然，围棋比我们能想象的简单得多。但与此同时，要达到 100% 逼真的物理会非常耗费算力。所以我们想创建一系列熔炉，其中有简单的、可以快速执行并迭代的，但我们仍然能看到非常复杂的行为。

turns.en: Interesting. Yeah. It's almost like what you choose to represent is tricky, right? Because for example, I can imagine a lot of economics arises from game theory, and most of that is completely unrelated to physics. So a crucible that represents physics is probably not that helpful. But if you have information theory represented—who knows what—then you probably do end up rediscovering quite a bit of economics. Is that a fair way to put it? Like the primitives you choose to capture in the environment kind of give rise to the type of learning that emerges.
turns.zh: 有趣。是的。这几乎就像你选择表示什么很棘手，对吧？因为例如，我可以想象很多经济学源于博弈论，而其中大部分与物理完全无关。所以一个表示物理的熔炉可能没那么有用。但如果你表示信息理论——谁知道呢——那么你很可能最终重新发现不少经济学。这样说公平吗？就像你在环境中选择捕捉的基本要素，会催生涌现出的学习类型。

turns.en: Yeah. Like the end goal is to have something that is grounded in the real world, right? But stepping stones.
turns.zh: 是的。最终目标是拥有一个扎根于现实世界的东西，对吧？但需要踏脚石。

turns.en: I wanted to come back to the Go example because I really like this example. You'll be surprised to hear that I find Go to be a good example. But what I find fascinating, which I think is what Lass is talking to here, is that Go is just a 19 by 19 grid where you're trying to maximize territory. And if this was a single agent game, it would be the most boring game you could imagine. It would be, you just place down stones on a grid until it fills up the whole grid, and there would be no strategy whatsoever. The moment you put a second agent into the environment, you get this emergent complexity because one agent has to reason about all the possible behaviors of the other agent. Suddenly it massively increases the complexity in the environment. And to the best of our knowledge, certainly all the compute which we sank into it when we were working on it, there was just this endless learning curve where without end you could continue to discover new things in this game.
turns.zh: 我想回到围棋的例子，因为我真的很喜欢这个例子。你会惊讶地听到我觉得围棋是个好例子。但我觉得迷人之处，也是我认为 Lass 在这里谈到的，是围棋只是一个 19x19 的网格，你试图最大化领地。如果这是单智能体游戏，它会是你想象中最无聊的游戏。你只是在网格上放棋子直到填满整个网格，没有任何策略。一旦你把第二个智能体放入环境，你就得到了这种涌现复杂性，因为一个智能体必须推理另一个智能体的所有可能行为。突然之间，它极大地增加了环境中的复杂性。据我们所知，当然还有我们研究它时投入的所有算力，存在一条无尽的学习曲线，你可以在这游戏中不断发现新事物。

turns.en: None of this is to say that Go is like the end point.
turns.zh: 这一切并不是说围棋就是终点。

turns.en: Of course, it's still just a board game and quite narrow in a certain sense, but it shows that very simple environment dynamics can lead to an infinite onion of layers of complexity that never stops — infinite to the capacity of what our computers can do, of course.
turns.zh: 当然，它仍然只是一个棋盘游戏，在某种意义上相当狭窄，但它表明，非常简单的环境动态可以导致一层又一层无穷无尽的复杂性，永不停歇——当然，其无限性受限于我们计算机的能力。

transcript.secZh: 棋盘游戏与无限复杂性

turns.en: Do you think that the agents will end up rediscovering language, and will that language look like ours or will it look different?
turns.zh: 你认为智能体最终会重新发现语言吗？那种语言会看起来像我们的语言，还是会有所不同？

turns.en: My personal belief is that anyone who thinks that human language is the endpoint of reasoning, or the best way to reason, that perspective is a little naive. I think it must be the case that there are far more sophisticated approaches to reasoning — maybe using parallelizable, rich, complex approaches, neural reasoning or whatever it is. These approaches will ultimately be far more expressive and far more capable than approaches which are based on human language.
turns.zh: 我个人的信念是，任何认为人类语言是推理的终点、或者是最好的推理方式的人，这种观点有点天真。我认为必然存在远比这更复杂的推理方法——也许使用可并行化、丰富、复杂的方法，神经推理或其他什么。这些方法最终将远比基于人类语言的方法更具表达力和能力。

turns.en: I would also say that starting from human language as the approach for reasoning is somewhat problematic because it pulls in all of our biases about how we think agents should think. So for example, a nice way to think about this is to imagine: what if we were to step back 500 years or a thousand years or 2,000 years and only were able to use all of the language that humans used at that time? So maybe our agents would believe that the world was flat, or that diseases were caused by the four humors, or there would be all kinds of strange beliefs that would be embedded in there and be very hard to remove because they're so fundamental to the language and the processes of thinking that humans have used. So I do think that going beyond this is a really important goal.
turns.zh: 我还想说，从人类语言出发作为推理的方法有些问题，因为它会引入我们关于智能体应该如何思考的所有偏见。举个例子，一个很好的思考方式是想象：如果我们退回到 500 年前、1000 年前或 2000 年前，只能使用当时人类使用的所有语言，会怎样？也许我们的智能体会相信世界是平的，或者疾病是由四种体液引起的，或者会有各种奇怪的信念嵌入其中，而且很难移除，因为它们对语言和人类所使用的思维过程来说太根本了。所以我确实认为，超越这一点是一个非常重要的目标。

transcript.secZh: 智能体会重新发现语言吗？

transcript.sec: Removing Human Priors: AlphaGo to AlphaZero

turns.en: I'd love to talk more about this concept of removing human priors. And I think your experience with AlphaGo, AlphaGo Zero is maybe the best example that anyone can point to of what happens when you remove human priors. Maybe if you take us back to AlphaGo and then AlphaZero, was it surprising to you that removing human priors would result in even smarter intelligence?
turns.zh: 我很想多谈谈这个移除人类先验的概念。我认为你在 AlphaGo、AlphaGo Zero 上的经历，也许是任何人能指出的、关于移除人类先验时会发生什么的最佳例子。也许你可以带我们回到 AlphaGo，然后是 AlphaZero，移除人类先验会带来更聪明的智能，这让你感到惊讶吗？

turns.en: I wasn't sure, honestly. I remember I always like to do things in research where you ask research questions which are on a knife edge, where it's like 50/50. I think it's not very interesting to do research where you already know the answer and you're like 95% certain this thing's going to work. It's kind of boring, honestly, to do those things. So I think good research is about asking questions where you're really not sure what the answer is in advance. And in this case, I was about 50/50 and I thought that maybe there was a good chance that it might. But I wasn't confident, and it was very exciting to see it.
turns.zh: 老实说，我并不确定。我记得我总是喜欢做那种研究，你提出的研究问题处于刀刃边缘，就像 50/50 一样。我认为做那种你已经知道答案、并且 95% 确定这东西会成功的研究，并不是很有趣。老实说，做那些事情有点无聊。所以我认为好的研究是关于提出你事先真的不确定答案的问题。在这个案例中，我大约是 50/50，我认为也许有很好的机会它会成功。但我并不自信，看到结果非常令人兴奋。

transcript.sec: The Bet on Giving Up Human Data

turns.en: I should say, you asked about human priors. So we are making a bet, and the bet we're making is that we can go further by giving up on the priors that everyone's relying on today — like the human data, the whole internet of knowledge that everyone else is building their systems upon. That's an important choice, and so we should probably talk about why we're doing that.
turns.zh: 我应该说明一下，你问到了人类先验。所以我们正在下一个赌注，我们下的赌注是：通过放弃今天所有人都在依赖的先验——比如人类数据，其他人都在其上构建系统的整个互联网知识——我们可以走得更远。这是一个重要的选择，所以我们可能应该谈谈为什么我们要这样做。

turns.en: I think the reason for me is, of course, it's a short-term sacrifice — we give up a certain amount of performance in order to access something which is potentially far greater. And it comes back to this: what does it mean to build a superlearner? To me, building a superlearner again is about building something that has this potential for full depth and breadth.
turns.zh: 我认为对我来说，原因当然是这是一种短期牺牲——我们放弃一定的性能，以获取可能远大得多的东西。这又回到了这一点：构建一个超级学习者意味着什么？对我来说，构建超级学习者就是构建具有全深度和全广度潜力的东西。

turns.en: So in the depth direction, we need to get to something which is capable of discovering things which go so far beyond human knowledge that it goes just far beyond the prior. And the more we lean on human data, the less able we are to actually discover the algorithms that are really going to take us all the way to something that's going to, for example, discover a whole new field of knowledge.
turns.zh: 所以在深度方向上，我们需要达到某种能够发现远远超越人类知识的东西，远远超越先验。我们越依赖人类数据，就越无法真正发现那些将带我们一路走向某种东西的算法，比如发现一个全新的知识领域。

turns.en: And then in the breadth direction, we need to have algorithms that can be placed down and discover things in environments for which language and human data that we've started with is just not a good fit. I mean, there are just many, many areas — different kinds of sensors, for example — where human language data or human data in general is not a good fit. And so I think by letting go of the human data, we put ourselves in a position where we can actually discover something which can go far, far beyond it.
turns.zh: 然后在广度方向上，我们需要有算法可以放置下去，在语言和我们开始时使用的人类数据根本不合适的环境中发现问题。我的意思是，有很多很多领域——例如不同类型的传感器——人类语言数据或一般的人类数据都不合适。所以我认为，通过放弃人类数据，我们让自己处于一个能够真正发现某种可以远远超越它的东西的位置。

transcript.sec: AlphaGo vs. AlphaZero: Two Years vs. a Few Hours

turns.en: And so if we come back to the AlphaGo example, what we found there was that the moment we let go of the human data — which we'd spent, by the way, about two years building AlphaGo, somewhat similar to the LLM approach, where we built every level of this, we hand put together the next level, we put in a lot of human data, and then we were human in the loop improving it, where we would take the previous generation and choose how we were going to improve it to give the next generation. And so we were right in the loop of this process. It took us two years to get to AlphaGo and beat Lee Sedol.
turns.zh: 所以如果我们回到 AlphaGo 的例子，我们发现的是：当我们放弃人类数据的那一刻——顺便说一句，我们花了大约两年时间构建 AlphaGo，有点类似于 LLM 的方法，我们构建了每一个层级，手工拼凑下一个层级，我们输入了大量人类数据，然后我们人在回路中改进它，我们会拿上一代并选择如何改进它以产生下一代。所以我们正处于这个过程的回路中。我们花了两年时间才达到 AlphaGo 并击败李世石。

turns.en: When we got AlphaZero right, we gave up on the human data and finally focused on what it would be like to build an algorithm that could discover for itself. So once we got it right, that algorithm took just a few hours — it took a few hours to outperform the two years of work which we'd done with human in the loop. So in the game of chess, it took four hours to beat the world champion, the best ever AI that had ever been created. In the game of Go, it took, I think it was a couple of days or something, but it was incredible progress. And so you have to let go of the human data to allow yourself to discover these things that can then shoot past the competition and discover the things that just keep learning and learning and learning forever.
turns.zh: 当我们把 AlphaZero 做对时，我们放弃了人类数据，最终专注于构建一种能够自我发现的算法会是什么样子。所以一旦我们做对了，那个算法只花了几个小时——几个小时就超越了我们在人在回路下所做的两年工作。所以在国际象棋中，它花了四个小时击败世界冠军，即当时有史以来创造的最好的 AI。在围棋中，我想花了几天左右，但这是令人难以置信的进步。所以你必须放弃人类数据，让自己发现这些东西，然后它们就能超越竞争，发现那些永远学习、学习、再学习的东西。

turns.en: So it has to be an active choice. And if you don't make that active choice, what I see in a lot of LLM companies today is they're basically building semi-autonomous human-in-the-loop learning algorithms, with thousands of people in the loop of the learning process. It works, and I have a lot of respect for how far it gets. But until we step back from that and really discover the process that's going to learn for itself, I don't believe we'll get all the way to something which is truly a super learner and unleashes the potential that we've talked about so far.
turns.zh: 所以这必须是一个主动的选择。如果你不做出这个主动选择，那么今天我在很多 LLM 公司看到的是，他们基本上是在构建半自主的人类在环学习算法，有成千上万的人参与到学习过程中。这确实有效，我也非常尊重它能达到的程度。但除非我们退后一步，真正发现那种能够自我学习的过程，否则我不相信我们能完全达到真正超级学习者的境界，并释放我们到目前为止所讨论的潜力。

turns.en: That's very profound. As far as I know, there are humans at Ineffable, and some of you are creating environments or crucibles. What does it look like to actually try and make sure that human priors aren't leaking into what you're doing?
turns.zh: 这非常深刻。据我所知，Ineffable 有真人参与，你们中的一些人正在创建环境或熔炉。那么，实际尝试确保人类先验不会渗入你们的工作中，会是什么样子？

transcript.secZh: 主动选择与人在回路学习

transcript.sec: Designing Environments and Avoiding Human Bias

turns.en: Yeah. Well, when we design environments and reward functions and so on, obviously there's a human bias in there. But we don't want to—as Dave was also mentioning earlier—we don't want to bias it towards building a machine based on, like, the von Neumann architecture or something like this. Right? We want to—but if you're stating some problem where a machine would be useful, it would be very interesting to see what type of machine it comes up with, like what computer-like machine it comes up with.
turns.zh: 是的。当我们设计环境和奖励函数等时，显然其中存在人类偏见。但我们不想——正如 Dave 之前也提到的——我们不想偏向于基于冯·诺依曼架构之类的机器来构建。对吧？我们想要——但如果你提出某个机器会有用的问题，那么看到它会想出什么类型的机器，比如什么样的计算机式机器，会非常有趣。

turns.en: So I totally agree with this. I would also say that we're not religious about this. It's not like a religion that you can't have any human prior anywhere. It's more like a pragmatic position that until we give up on relying on the trillion-item data sets of human knowledge, we're not going to make the progress that the field deserves to see. So it's more like a practical position. And so in practice, of course there's going to be a certain amount of prior which, as Lassa says, will apply to many different worlds, as opposed to trying to put in these very strong priors that exactly encode all the knowledge we know about this one particular problem or this one particular world. So kind of weak, environment-agnostic priors seem perfectly reasonable, but these super strong priors with trillion-item data sets—we're trying to avoid that because we think pragmatically it's going to lead to better outcomes.
turns.zh: 所以我完全同意这一点。我还要说，我们对此并不教条。这不是一种宗教，认为任何地方都不能有人类先验。这更像是一种务实的立场：除非我们放弃依赖万亿项的人类知识数据集，否则我们不会取得该领域应得的进展。所以这更像是一种实际立场。在实践中，当然会有一定量的先验，正如 Lassa 所说，这些先验将适用于许多不同的世界，而不是试图放入这些非常强的先验，精确编码我们所知道的关于这个特定问题或这个特定世界的所有知识。所以，弱的环境无关先验似乎完全合理，但那些带有万亿项数据集的超强先验——我们试图避免，因为我们认为从务实角度这会带来更好的结果。

transcript.secZh: 设计环境与避免人类偏见

turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. You mentioned that you like philosophically that you're drawn to research that's more on a knife's edge 50/50. I'm curious what your confidence levels are for, you know, Ineffable broad at the broadest level—like does a super learner emerge? And then I guess at the more pragmatic level in terms of the things that you're trying to accomplish right now. Are you 50/50 on these as well?
turns.zh: 是的，绝对。你提到从哲学上讲，你被吸引到更处于刀刃边缘的 50/50 研究。我很好奇你的信心水平，你知道，Ineffable 在最广泛的层面上——比如超级学习者会出现吗？然后我想在更务实的层面上，就你们现在试图实现的事情而言。你对这些也是 50/50 吗？

turns.en: So first of all, I would say I strongly believe that the approach will be feasible at some point. Like we—in fact, it's the only thing for which we have an example. Like, you know, the example in our brains is the only existence proof of something which has discovered an incredible intelligence that's very general and works in embodied world and discovers how to do all kinds of different things. So we have this incredible example of the human brain that we can look at. So then, do I think we can achieve it? Well, I think like many great moments in science, it's about timing. So whether this succeeds or fails, I think is about timing. When you create a startup, you want to be at the right time. You don't want to be too early or too late. If you're too late, everyone's done it. It's not interesting—like a thousand other people have already done it. And if you're too early, you might be banging on the door, but not have the right kind of—maybe the field isn't advanced enough or there isn't enough compute to be able to succeed yet. So to me, it's all about timing. For example, with Computer Go, I made a prediction I think 10 years before Computer Go was solved, and I got it right to the year. Got it right for Starcraft, which I also—we had a bet and made a prediction. Same for AlphaProof when we predicted when the IMO was going to fall.
turns.zh: 首先，我会说，我坚信这种方法在某个时候会变得可行。就像我们——事实上，这是我们唯一有例子的东西。比如，我们大脑中的例子是唯一的存在证明，证明某种东西已经发现了令人难以置信的智能，这种智能非常通用，在具身世界中有效，并发现如何做各种不同的事情。所以我们有这个人脑的惊人例子，我们可以观察。那么，我认为我们能实现它吗？嗯，我认为像科学中许多伟大时刻一样，这关乎时机。所以无论这成功还是失败，我认为都关乎时机。当你创建一家初创公司时，你想在正确的时间。你不想太早或太晚。如果你太晚，每个人都做过了。这没意思——就像其他一千个人已经做过了。如果你太早，你可能在敲门，但没有正确的——也许领域不够先进，或者没有足够的算力来成功。所以对我来说，一切都关乎时机。例如，在计算机围棋方面，我在计算机围棋被解决前 10 年做出了预测，我精确到年份。星际争霸也是如此，我也——我们打赌并做出了预测。AlphaProof 也是如此，当我们预测 IMO 何时会被攻克时。

transcript.sec: Super Forecasting and the Right Time

turns.en: So you're a super forecaster of sorts.
turns.zh: 所以你算是某种超级预测者。

turns.en: So far, so far I've done very well at this. And I do have a very strong sense that this is the right time for this to fall, but that super learners are possible. Like there's been enormous progress in the level of technology, the ability to accelerate research using LLM coding methods or auto research methods like we've produced in the past, the ability and understanding of scaling laws, and the sophistication of technology and the stack. There's a lot of things that fall into place that I think make this the right time. So that's my bet—that this is the right timing. But yeah, of course, look, this is research.
turns.zh: 到目前为止，到目前为止我在这方面做得很好。我确实有强烈的感觉，这是实现这一目标的正确时机，超级学习者是可能的。就像技术水平取得了巨大进步，使用 LLM 编码方法或我们过去产生的自动研究方法加速研究的能力，对缩放定律的理解和能力，以及技术和堆栈的复杂性。有很多事情都到位了，我认为这使现在成为正确时机。所以这是我的赌注——这是正确的时机。但当然，看，这是研究。

turns.en: Research is never guaranteed, and that's what makes it exciting. If you get the timing right, you can be the first. You can be the ones to change the whole field of AI, and that's what it means to take risks and do something exciting.
turns.zh: 研究从来不是保证的，这正是它令人兴奋的地方。如果你把握对了时机，你可以成为第一个。你可以成为改变整个 AI 领域的人，这就是冒险和做令人兴奋的事情的意义。

transcript.sec: Compute as a Driver of Timing

turns.en: For Ineffable and also all the previous things that you correctly forecasted, is the biggest driver of timing compute?
turns.zh: 对于 Ineffable 以及你之前正确预测的所有事情，时机最大的驱动因素是算力吗？

turns.en: I think it's a very big driver. I think it's an enormous driver. I think, yeah, I mean, we're in a great position with the compute that we've managed to get hold of, and I think it gives an opportunity to do things which are orders of magnitude more sophisticated than approaches that have tried to do self-discovered RL in the past. So I think, yeah, if we compare to, I don't know, something like hide-and-seek from OpenAI, which was an early example where agents discovered some basic tool use, I think we could probably run experiments that use 100,000 times more compute. And so it's kind of amazing that people haven't come back and really pushed on these types of approaches given the availability of compute. And of course, hide-and-seek—I don't want to pretend that that's the end goal.
turns.zh: 我认为这是一个非常大的驱动因素。我认为这是一个巨大的驱动因素。我认为，是的，我的意思是，我们凭借设法获得的算力处于有利位置，我认为这提供了机会去做比过去尝试自发现强化学习的方法复杂几个数量级的事情。所以我认为，是的，如果我们比较，我不知道，像 OpenAI 的 hide-and-seek 这样的东西，这是一个早期例子，智能体发现了基本的工具使用，我认为我们可能可以运行使用 10 万倍算力的实验。所以有点惊人，人们没有回来真正推动这些类型的方法，考虑到算力的可用性。当然，hide-and-seek——我不想假装那是最终目标。

transcript.secZh: 算力作为时机的驱动因素

turns.en: I think it's very basic, but I think it's suggestive of what could be done. I think compute is a huge driver, but that's not the only one.
turns.zh: 我觉得这很基础，但它暗示了可以做什么。我认为算力是一个巨大的驱动力，但不是唯一的。

turns.en: I think we're in a very fortunate situation that we have been able to secure a very large cluster.
turns.zh: 我认为我们处于非常幸运的境地，我们能够获得一个非常大的集群。

turns.en: A beautiful cluster at that.
turns.zh: 而且是一个漂亮的集群。

turns.en: Yeah, so this is really an opportunity for us. We really have the cars on our hands to test this out. Very few other people are doing something similar. So yeah, we can really test this out in a way that we couldn't do at DeepMind, for instance.
turns.zh: 是的，所以这对我们来说真的是一个机会。我们真的手头有车可以测试这个。很少有其他人做类似的事情。所以是的，我们可以真正测试这个，这是我们在 DeepMind 无法做到的。

turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对。

turns.en: It seems like one of the maybe determinants of how far this can go is how far you can push simulation and because ultimately these crucibles are digital, right? And I think simulation has probably come quite far in the last handful of years. But it's not perfect, right? We recently had your friend Rich Sutton on the show and I asked him about simulation and he said he was very dismissive of simulation. I'm curious how you guys think about this and Lisa, you've been on both sides of this. I think you obviously did a lot in the digital world. But you also built MetNet which touches real world atmospheric data. How do you all think about where is the ceiling on simulation and what is when is the right time to bring an Apple into the real world?
turns.zh: 看起来这可能走多远的决定因素之一是你能把模拟推到多远，因为最终这些熔炉是数字的，对吧？我认为模拟在过去几年可能已经走了很远。但它并不完美，对吧？我们最近请了你的朋友 Rich Sutton 上节目，我问了他关于模拟的问题，他说他对模拟非常不屑。我很好奇你们怎么想这个，Lisa，你在这两方面都有经验。我认为你显然在数字世界做了很多。但你也构建了 MetNet，它触及真实世界的大气数据。你们怎么想模拟的上限在哪里，什么时候是把苹果带入真实世界的正确时机？

turns.en: So I guess MetNet was actually an example. So this is a weather forecasting model we did in the Google Brain Amsterdam office together with Google Research where we were doing a machine learning model to predict short term weather forecasts and this was way better than the physics based simulations. So the physics simulations were accumulating errors over time so there's a point to that that physics simulation is not perfect. I do think there's a lot of relatively simple environments that we can build where we can see this emerging behavior of let's say technology and so on where we don't need exact physics. I actually do think it's interesting to see how much we can build these days with a very small team in terms of these simulations and so on. So there's definitely a ceiling.
turns.zh: 所以我想 MetNet 实际上是一个例子。这是我们在 Google Brain 阿姆斯特丹办公室与 Google Research 一起做的天气预报模型，我们做一个机器学习模型来预测短期天气预报，这比基于物理的模拟要好得多。所以物理模拟会随着时间的推移累积错误，所以物理模拟并不完美。我确实认为我们可以构建很多相对简单的环境，在那里我们可以看到这种新兴行为，比如技术等等，我们不需要精确的物理。我实际上认为有趣的是看看这些天我们可以用非常小的团队在模拟等方面构建多少。所以肯定有一个上限。

turns.en: Is there a ceiling actually? I'm curious about this.
turns.zh: 实际上有上限吗？我很好奇这个。

turns.en: Well, I guess quantum physics and whatnot, right? But so there's a ceiling somewhere but we can do very interesting things without real physics I would say.
turns.zh: 嗯，我想是量子物理之类的，对吧？但所以某个地方有上限，但我想说我们可以在没有真实物理的情况下做非常有趣的事情。

turns.en: So I think the right question to ask is can a superintelligence be built in simulation. So if it is possible for it to be built in simulation I believe it will happen 10 times or 100 times faster just because simulation can be infinitely parallelized. You get perfect reproducibility. It has a lot of really nice properties. It's also the safest place for a superintelligence to be built. So it has these really nice properties. Then we need to ask is it possible? And I think for the reasons we discussed earlier, there are very clear approaches that we can add into the simulation that allow it to be sufficiently complex to represent arbitrarily interesting things. So for example like let's say you wanted to build a computer in simulation well all you require is that your simulation is Turing complete if you have a Turing complete simulation suddenly everything that we mean by computation like everything like provably everything we mean by computation can be expressed completely inside simulation and indeed humans have built incredibly complex computers or related things inside simulated worlds. The same is true for various other ideas like you know if you want to build an economy like you know money can be built out of coins or out of paper or out of bits and as long as you have one of those you know some representation of money everything that we mean by economics can be expressed inside a simulation. The same is true for language. If you've got multiple agents and they've got some ability to express a channel of communication between the agents, suddenly everything that we mean by language is expressible in simulation. Mathematics we know is expressible in any universe. Science in some sense is the study of our world. So will a simulation be sufficient to study what we mean by science? Well, there are some aspects of science which are expressible in many things like you know energy or entropy or evolution. But also it's true that you know the agent will discover its own science. Like whatever the simulator is, if it's got this emergent complexity to its environment, the agent will discover its own science about whatever that world is. It's very like provably possible to build environments in which it's possible to express and represent enormous complexity of all of these things.
turns.zh: 所以我认为正确的问题是能否在模拟中构建超级智能。所以如果可以在模拟中构建它，我相信它会快 10 倍或 100 倍发生，因为模拟可以无限并行化。你得到完美的可重复性。它有很多非常好的特性。它也是构建超级智能最安全的地方。所以它有这些非常好的特性。然后我们需要问这可能吗？我认为根据我们之前讨论的原因，我们可以将非常清晰的方法添加到模拟中，使其足够复杂以表示任意有趣的事物。例如，假设你想在模拟中构建一台计算机，那么你所需要的只是你的模拟是图灵完备的，如果你有一个图灵完备的模拟，突然我们所说的计算的一切，比如一切，可证明我们所说的计算的一切都可以完全在模拟中表达，事实上人类已经在模拟世界中构建了极其复杂的计算机或相关事物。同样适用于各种其他想法，比如你知道如果你想建立一个经济体，你知道钱可以用硬币或纸或比特来构建，只要你有其中一个，你知道钱的某种表示，我们所说的经济学的一切都可以在模拟中表达。语言也是如此。如果你有多个智能体，并且它们有某种能力来表达智能体之间的通信渠道，突然我们所说的语言的一切都可以在模拟中表达。我们知道数学可以在任何宇宙中表达。科学在某种意义上是研究我们的世界。那么模拟是否足以研究我们所说的科学？嗯，科学有一些方面可以在许多事物中表达，比如你知道能量或熵或进化。但同样真实的是，你知道智能体会发现自己的科学。就像无论模拟器是什么，如果它的环境具有这种涌现的复杂性，智能体将发现关于那个世界的自己的科学。非常可证明的是，可以构建环境，在其中可以表达和表示所有这些事物的巨大复杂性。

turns.en: Well, I agree with Lassa. There might be some things which aren't well expressed. You know there will be things which can only be expressed in the real world like quantum computation is a good example. The real point is that if it's possible to get all the way to a superintelligence in simulation it will happen faster and it will happen safer and so for those reasons it's something that we choose to put a lot of energy into. I actually agree with Rich Sutton that you know I think his point was something along the lines that you shouldn't expect that the things that you learn in simulation to like transfer like sim to real into the real world because the real world is like just like vastly more complex and in very interesting ways that hard to simulate. But I think what we can do is we can do all of the science to discover the superlearner. And once we have that superlearner we will have the answers and we'll know how to build something which that same algorithm should be applicable to the real world and we can also you know make our simulations more and more high-fidelity towards the real world and check that they still work before putting them into the world.
turns.zh: 嗯，我同意 Lassa。可能有一些东西不能很好地表达。你知道会有一些东西只能在真实世界中表达，比如量子计算就是一个很好的例子。真正的要点是，如果有可能在模拟中一路走到超级智能，它会更快发生，也会更安全发生，所以出于这些原因，这是我们选择投入大量精力的事情。我实际上同意 Rich Sutton，你知道我认为他的观点是，你不应该期望在模拟中学到的东西能像 sim-to-real 一样转移到真实世界，因为真实世界就像更复杂得多，并且以非常有趣的方式难以模拟。但我认为我们可以做的是，我们可以做所有的科学来发现超级学习者。一旦我们有了那个超级学习者，我们就会有答案，我们就会知道如何构建一些东西，同样的算法应该适用于真实世界，我们也可以让我们的模拟越来越接近真实世界的高保真度，并在将它们放入世界之前检查它们是否仍然有效。
